analysis.one_liner: Raises the legal bar for the DEA to immediately suspend drug distributors' registrations.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote on July 29, 2014, but the Senate never acted and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites parts of the Controlled Substances Act that let the Attorney General crack down on companies licensed to handle controlled substances. It defines 'imminent danger' so narrowly that the DEA can order an immediate suspension only when controlled substances will keep being intentionally diverted or dispensed in a way that poses a present or foreseeable risk of serious harm or death [S3][S4]. Before revoking or suspending any registration, the DEA must serve a written order with specific legal citations, give the registrant at least 30 days, and invite the company to submit a 'corrective action plan' that can get proceedings discontinued or deferred [S3][S4]. It also directs federal health agencies to report on obstacles to patient access to controlled substances [S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Registered drug distributors, pharmacies, and manufacturers facing DEA enforcement proceedings gain the most: they get guaranteed written notice, a 30-day window, and a chance to submit a corrective action plan that can get revocation or suspension dropped or delayed [S3][S4]. The DEA's emergency suspension power is narrowed to cases where diversion is intentional, ongoing, and poses a foreseeable risk of serious harm or death [S3][S4]. Supporters said legitimate pain patients would benefit if enforcement were better targeted at truly bad actors instead of sweeping up compliant pharmacies and doctors [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drug distributors and pharmacies under DEA scrutiny

how_it_helps.text: Gives any registrant facing denial, revocation, or suspension a written order stating the basis with specific legal citations, an appearance date no sooner than 30 days out, and notice of the right to submit a corrective action plan [S3][S4].

Requires the Attorney General to review any corrective action plan and decide whether to discontinue or defer the enforcement proceedings, giving companies a built-in path to avoid losing their registration [S3][S4].

Narrows 'imminent danger' for immediate suspension to substances that will continue to be intentionally diverted or dispensed outside professional practice with a present or foreseeable risk of serious adverse health consequences or death [S3][S4].

Directs HHS, FDA, and CDC to report to Congress on obstacles to legitimate patient access to controlled substances and on collaboration between law enforcement and the pharmaceutical industry [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: The costs fall on the DEA's enforcement capacity and, indirectly, on communities affected by prescription drug diversion: when the emergency suspension tool applies to fewer situations and companies get a mandatory negotiation period before any revocation, suspicious shipments and problem registrants can keep operating longer [S3][S4]. Taxpayers also fund the new federal study and report on patient access [S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: The DEA and communities facing drug diversion

drawbacks.text: The redefined 'imminent danger' standard means the DEA can no longer immediately suspend a registration merely because controlled substances are being diverted; it must show diversion is intentional, ongoing, and carries a foreseeable risk of serious harm or death, which narrows the agency's fastest enforcement tool [S3][S4].

The mandatory 30-day show-cause period and the corrective action plan process can delay revocation or suspension for months while a registrant keeps distributing controlled substances; proceedings against a plan can be 'deferred for the purposes of modification' indefinitely [S3][S4].

Supporters' strongest objection to these concerns was that legitimate pharmacies, wholesalers, and pain physicians were losing registrations over paperwork and compliance disputes, cutting off real patients' access to medication — the bill's stated purpose was protecting that access [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real due-process protections to registrants, and some of those protections serve legitimate businesses caught up in enforcement disputes. But its core effect is to raise the legal bar against the DEA's strongest enforcement actions — the immediate suspension of a registration — and to build in a mandatory negotiation phase before revocation. Given that prescription opioid diversion was a growing public health problem, shifting leverage from the enforcement agency toward the regulated distributors was a cost that fell on the public, while the benefit to patients was indirect and depended on enforcement being poorly targeted in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote in July 2014, the Senate sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and no one ever brought it to the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Energy and Commerce Committee marked the bill up in June 2014 and ordered it reported as amended by voice vote [S6].
On July 29, 2014, the House passed the amended bill by voice vote under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure used for noncontroversial bills [S6][S1].

The Senate received the bill on July 30, 2014, and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where no further action was taken before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S6][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The DEA's existing enforcement authority over drug distributors stayed intact through the end of the 113th Congress, so the agency and the public it protects were better off than they would have been under this bill. Registered distributors, pharmacies, and manufacturers remained better off than they would have been had the Senate passed it — though a nearly identical version of this same bill did become law two years later, in 2016, and is the version widely credited with weakening DEA enforcement during the opioid epidemic.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: DEA enforcement stayed intact for now

sides.party_line_note: The bill passed the House by voice vote with no recorded opposition, and its 12 cosponsors were 10 Republicans and 2 Democrats; no senators are recorded as taking any position before it died in committee.

industries.note: Distributors of controlled substances facing DEA enforcement would gain guaranteed notice, a 30-day window, and a corrective action plan route that can discontinue or defer revocation proceedings, while the immediate suspension tool would apply to fewer situations [S3][S4]. Weaker enforcement means suspicious shipments of addictive painkillers can keep flowing longer, a cost borne by the public.

Registrants that dispense controlled substances would get due-process protections before losing their DEA registration. Supporters framed this as protecting legitimate pain patients from losing access, but the same protections shield registrants whose licenses the DEA is trying to pull for diversion [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Drug enforcement (DEA) and state and local law enforcement
industries.note: The bill narrows the legal standard for immediately suspending a registration and adds mandatory procedural steps before revocation, reducing the agency's fastest tools against problem registrants [S3][S4]. The bill also folds the pharmaceutical industry into a federally commissioned report on enforcement and access, treating distributors as stakeholders rather than enforcement targets [S4].
